title: House & Its Subgenres: Deep, Tech, Soulful, Disco
skill: Identify house subgenres by BPM and feel and mix them using their long, DJ-friendly intros and outros.
content:
What house is built on

House is a 4/4 genre defined by a steady kick on every quarter note, an offbeat open hi-hat (the 'tss' on the 'and' of each beat), and a syncopated bass and clap on the 2 and 4. It was born in Chicago in the early 1980s from disco edits played on drum machines. Almost every house record is mixed in tools-first format: a long DJ intro of drums only, a main section with the hook, a breakdown, and a long drum outro. That structure is the gift to the DJ — you have 16 to 32 bars of beats with no melody at each end to overlap cleanly.

The family at a glance

SubgenreBPMFeel / signature
Deep house118-124Warm Rhodes chords, dubby bass, restrained, hypnotic
Tech house122-128Stripped, percussive, rolling bass, minimal melody, club-driven
Soulful / vocal house120-126Live-feel chords, gospel and soul vocals, rich keys
Disco / nu-disco / French115-124Sampled strings, filtered loops, live bass and guitar, funky
Classic / Chicago / jackin120-127Raw 909 drums, big organ stabs, vocal chops

How to tell them apart by ear

  • Deep house sits back — the bass is round and dubby, chords are jazzy and slightly detuned, and nothing fights for attention. If it feels like a 2am warm-up, it is deep.
  • Tech house leans forward — the groove is busy, the bass is a tight rolling 8th-note line, and there is almost no melody, just percussion and a vocal snippet. It is built for peak-time energy.
  • Soulful foregrounds a real or sampled vocal and lush keys; the swing is looser and more musical.
  • Disco brings recognizable samples, filter sweeps that open across 8 bars, and a funky live bassline.

Mixing conventions

House is the most forgiving genre to learn long blends on. Use the EQ blend and bass swap as your default. Bring the incoming track in on its drum intro, low-cut so its bass does not clash. Let it run 16 to 32 bars over the outgoing track's outro. At a phrase boundary, swap the bass: cut the low EQ on the outgoing deck and open it on the incoming one in a single move. Because intros and outros are pure drums, you can sit in the overlap for a long time without two melodies clashing.

Mind the swing. Some deep and disco tracks carry significant swing (a shuffled hi-hat), while tech house is usually dead straight. A swung track over a straight one can sound 'flammy' even when the beatgrid is perfect — trust your ears over SYNC and nudge to lock the hats, not just the kicks.

Energy and key

Within a set, treat BPM as your energy dial: warm up at 120 deep, push to 125-127 tech house at peak. Keep transitions inside two BPM of each other so pitch shift stays invisible. House mixes so smoothly that harmonic clashes become the thing the crowd hears — use the Camelot wheel to stay in compatible keys, especially when two melodic chord stabs overlap in the breakdown.

Common gotcha

The long breakdowns in deep and progressive-leaning house can tempt you to mix during them. Avoid it — a breakdown has no kick to anchor phase, and the crowd is waiting for the drop. Always bring your next track in on drums, over an outro or main groove, never over a breakdown's empty space.
exercise: Mix three house subgenres in a row to feel the energy climb. Start with a deep house track around 120 BPM, blend into a tech house track at 125 using a 32-bar drum-intro overlap and a clean bass swap at the phrase, then bring in a disco-flavoured track and ride its filter sweep into the next groove. Keep every transition within two BPM and listen for hi-hat swing clashes.

tracks.why: Classic Chicago house with a long pure-drum intro and steady groove — the ideal first long blend.

title: Techno: Energy & Mixing
skill: Mix techno with long hypnotic blends and layered loops that suit its driving, stripped-back energy.
content:
The aesthetic of techno

Techno is relentless, hypnotic, and stripped to its functional core: a hard 4/4 kick, sparse percussion, and texture instead of melody. Where house grooves and swings, techno drives — the kick is heavier and more forward, the synths are atmospheric drones or stabs, and the whole track is designed to put the dancefloor in a trance through repetition. There is rarely a 'hook' to wait for; the energy is in the layers slowly being added and stripped away.

The tempo map

StyleBPMCharacter
Dub / deep techno120-126Spacious, reverb-heavy, hypnotic, Berlin/Detroit lineage
Peak-time / 'big room' techno128-134Driving, distorted kicks, festival energy
Hard / industrial techno135-150Aggressive, raw, fast, rave-leaning
Hypnotic / minimal126-132Loop-based, subtle evolution, very long mixes

Why techno mixing is different

Because techno tracks are loops with little melodic content, you can blend them for far longer than house — 48, 64, even 96 bars is normal. The art is in layering: you are not just handing over the floor, you are stacking two tracks so a new percussion line or stab from deck B rides on top of deck A's groove before you let the first one go. This creates rhythms that exist in neither track alone.

Long hypnotic blends, step by step

  1. Cue deck B's drum intro on its downbeat and beatmatch by ear — techno is unforgiving of drift over a long blend, so check phase every 16 bars.
  2. Bring B in with the low EQ cut so the two kicks never stack and turn to mud.
  3. Let the two grooves run together for many bars. Use the high and mid EQs to weave B's hats and stabs in and out over A's groove.
  4. When you are ready to commit, do the bass swap at a phrase: cut A's lows, open B's in one move.
  5. Filter or echo A out rather than just pulling the fader — a hard cut breaks the hypnotic spell.
One kick at a time. Two techno kicks playing together is the single most common rookie mistake. They are loud, sustained and central — overlap them and the mix sounds like a dropped phone. Keep deck B low-cut until the exact moment you swap, then take A's lows fully out.

Layering loops and tension

Use your mixer or software loop function to grab a 1, 2, or 4-bar loop from deck A, then build a transition under it while you cue B. The filter is your most important tool in techno: roll the high-pass filter up across 8-16 bars to thin a track to a hiss before a drop, then slam it back open on the downbeat. Reverb and delay 'throws' on a single hit extend the trance. Avoid busy beat juggling — techno wants restraint and patience, not flash.

Energy management

You cannot ride a melodic peak in techno the way you can in trance — there usually isn't one. Instead you manage energy with density and tempo: add layers and creep the BPM up by one or two over several tracks to lift the room, then strip back to a single kick and a dub chord to give breathing space before building again.
exercise: Practice a 64-bar hypnotic blend. Load two driving techno tracks within one BPM of each other, beatmatch by ear, and run them together for 64 bars while you weave deck B's percussion in with the high and mid EQ, keeping its bass cut the whole time. Swap the bass at a phrase boundary, then filter-fade the outgoing track away rather than cutting it.

tracks.why: A pure percussion loop track that teaches layering and long blends with almost no melody to clash.

tracks.title: The Bells

title: Trance & Progressive
skill: Mix trance and progressive using their breakdown/build structure to ride emotional peaks.
content:
Music built around the breakdown

Trance and progressive are the most structurally dramatic dance genres. Where techno hypnotizes through repetition, trance tells a story with a clear arc: a driving intro, a long emotional breakdown where the drums drop out and a melody or vocal swells, a building riser with a snare roll, and an explosive drop back into the full groove. The DJ's job is to use that structure — to land your next track's breakdown at exactly the right emotional moment.

Tempo and style

StyleBPMCharacter
Progressive house / trance124-128Long evolving builds, rolling bass, subtle, hypnotic melody
Uplifting / euphoric trance132-140Big supersaw leads, emotional breakdowns, anthemic
Psytrance140-150Rolling 16th-note bass, dark or psychedelic, driving
Tech / progressive trance128-134Tighter, club-focused, less melodic, more groove

The structure you mix around

A typical uplifting trance track runs: 32-bar intro (drums and bass), 32-64 bars of groove, a 32-64 bar breakdown (kick drops out, pads and lead swell), an 8-16 bar build (rising riser, snare roll, the kick teases back in), then the drop where the full energy and lead hit together. This is your map. The classic trance transition is to start mixing during your current track's outro or final groove so the incoming track's breakdown begins just as you complete the bass swap — the crowd gets a fresh emotional lift exactly when the old track finishes.

The breakdown blend

  1. Beatmatch deck B during deck A's main groove, low EQ cut.
  2. Time it so deck B enters and its breakdown arrives as deck A reaches its end.
  3. During the breakdown there is no kick — let the pads and melody of both tracks blend, watching harmonic key so the two leads do not clash (this is where the Camelot wheel matters most).
  4. As deck B's riser and snare roll build, pull A out entirely so the drop hits clean with only B playing.
  5. The drop on the downbeat is the payoff — let it land alone, full energy.
Harmonic mixing is mandatory here. Two trance leads overlapping in a breakdown will expose any key clash instantly — it is the most melodic, exposed moment in dance music. Mix in the same key or one step around the wheel, or your beautiful breakdown turns sour.

Riding the peak and using FX

The filter and the reverb/echo are your emotional tools. Sweep a high-pass filter up through a build to add tension, then drop it open on the downbeat. A long reverb tail on the last melody note before a drop creates a moment of suspension. Resist mixing through a drop — the drop is the climax, so let it breathe. In progressive (the calmer cousin), blends are longer and subtler; you ride evolving energy rather than explosive peaks, and you can sit in long overlaps like techno.

Pacing the set

Trance is a journey genre. Plan your set as a rising line of energy with deliberate dips: after a huge euphoric drop, bring in something with a longer breakdown to reset the room before the next peak. Never play two massive anthems back to back — the contrast is what makes a peak feel like a peak.
exercise: Execute one breakdown-to-drop transition. Beatmatch an incoming trance track under a current one, time it so the incoming breakdown begins as the current track ends, blend the two melodic breakdowns in a compatible key, then ride the riser and pull the old track out so the drop lands with only the new track playing. Use a high-pass filter sweep through the build for extra tension.

tracks.why: A textbook trance arc with a long emotional breakdown and clean build — perfect for practicing breakdown-to-drop timing.

title: Drum & Bass / Jungle
skill: Mix drum & bass and jungle at 170+ BPM using double-drops and breakdown blends.
content:
Fast drums, slow bass

Drum & bass runs at 170-176 BPM, but it does not feel twice as fast as house — the secret is that the bassline and the overall groove sit at half that tempo (around 85), while a chopped breakbeat skitters on top at full speed. This 'fast drums over slow bass' feel is the genre's identity. Jungle, its early-90s ancestor, leans harder on chopped Amen and Think breaks, ragga vocal samples, and heavy sub; modern DnB ranges from rolling liquid to aggressive neurofunk.

The spectrum

StyleBPMCharacter
Jungle / ragga jungle160-170Chopped breaks, heavy sub, reggae/ragga samples
Liquid DnB170-174Smooth, musical, vocals, rolling drums
Neurofunk / techy172-176Dark, complex basses, surgical drums
Jump-up172-176Bouncy, rave-y, big wobble basses, crowd energy

The DnB intro is your friend

Almost every DnB track has a 16 or 32-bar intro of drums and a simple beat — no bass — explicitly built for mixing. The standard DnB transition is the breakdown blend: bring the incoming track in on this drum intro, beatmatched, and let it roll over the outgoing track's first 'roll-out' (the section after its drop where it returns to drums). Because the bass is what defines a DnB track, the cardinal rule is that only one bass plays at a time — drop the new bass at a phrase as you pull the old one.

The double-drop

The signature DnB move is the double-drop: timing two tracks so both their drops hit on the exact same downbeat, doubling the impact. Done right it is the most explosive moment a DJ can create; done a beat off it is a trainwreck.

  1. Cue both tracks so you know exactly how many bars from a marked cue each drop is.
  2. Beatmatch perfectly — at 174 BPM, even a slight drift ruins the alignment.
  3. Count the phrasing so both drops land on the same '1'.
  4. Use the EQ to make sure the two basses do not both blast at the drop — favour one bass and let the other's drums and mids fill the rest.
  5. After the double-drop, pick a winner and pull the other track.
Beatmatch by ear at speed. SYNC drift is far more audible at 174 than at 124 because there are more transients per second. Train your ear to nudge the jog and trust the snare crack alignment, not just the kicks — DnB snares are loud and land on the 2 and 4, so they are your best phase reference.

Energy and selection

DnB sets move fast — tracks are often mixed in and out within a minute or two, so you are always cueing the next one. Manage energy by moving between rolling/liquid and harder neuro/jump-up sections. The half-time/double-time relationship also makes DnB a perfect bridge genre: a 174 track read as 87 can blend the drums of a hip-hop or dubstep track, which the next lesson and lesson 7 explore.
exercise: Land one double-drop. Pick two DnB tracks at the same BPM, mark a cue exactly 16 bars before each track's drop, beatmatch by ear using the snare on the 2 and 4, and bring the second track in so both drops hit the same downbeat. Favour one bassline with the EQ at the drop, then pull the losing track.

title: Dubstep / Bass / Trap
skill: Mix dubstep, bass and trap with half-time feel and big drop-focused transitions.
content:
The half-time feel

Dubstep and trap are defined by half-time drums: the tempo grid is fast, but the snare lands on the 3 instead of the 2 and 4, so the beat feels half as fast as the number suggests. Dubstep is gridded at 140 BPM but feels like 70. Trap is gridded around 140-150 but feels like 70-75, with rattling triplet hi-hats and 808 sub-bass. This spacious, heavy feel is the whole point — it leaves room for huge, distorted bass 'drops' that are the emotional centre of every track.

The bass-music family

StyleBPM (grid / feel)Signature
Dubstep140 / 70Wobble and growl bass, snare on the 3, big drops
Trap140-150 / 70-75808 sub, triplet/rolling hats, rap-influenced
Riddim140-150 / 70-75Repetitive metallic bass, minimal, heavy
Future bass140-160 / 70-80Detuned supersaw chords, vocal chops, melodic
Garage / 2-step / UKG130-140Swung shuffle, skippy drums, soulful

Mixing around the drop

Bass music is drop-focused, so transitions are built around drops, not long blends. Two heavy, distorted bass drops layered together turn to noise — these tracks are mixed sparse-section to sparse-section. The standard transition is to bring the new track in during a build or a calmer 'second drop' section, then cut to it on the downbeat of the new drop. You are handing over on the breakdowns and intros, not over the heavy parts.

Practical transition methods

  1. Drop swap: let track A play through its drop, mix B's intro in during A's post-drop calm, and slam to B at B's drop downbeat. The crowd never hears two drops at once.
  2. Build-to-drop: use B's riser/build as the transition, cutting A out under the riser so B's drop lands alone — exactly like the trance build, but heavier.
  3. FX cut: echo-out or reverb-throw the end of A's drop, leave a beat of silence, then drop B. The momentary gap actually heightens impact in bass music.
Beatmatch the half-time, mix the full grid. Because the kick and snare are sparse, beatmatch using the hi-hats or the underlying grid, not the slow snare — there are not enough snare hits per bar to lock phase quickly. Set your software grid to the true 140, even though the song feels like 70.

Trap, 808s and crowd energy

Trap leans heavily on the 808 — a long, tuned sub kick that doubles as the bassline. When mixing two trap tracks, watch for 808 clash: a held 808 in one key over another track is dissonant and muddy, so cut lows aggressively and favour one 808 at a time. Trap and bass sets are about impact and contrast: a stretch of high-energy drops, then a melodic future-bass or vocal moment to breathe, then back in.

Bridging tempos

The half-time feel makes bass music a natural bridge between tempo worlds. A 140 dubstep track shares a feel with 70 BPM hip-hop, and its grid can lock to 140 house or even pitch into the 170s for DnB by treating its feel as half-time — the cross-genre lesson covers these tricks in depth.
exercise: Build a drop-swap transition. Play a dubstep or trap track through its first drop, beatmatch the next track on the underlying 140 grid using the hi-hats, mix its intro in during the calm after the first drop, then cut hard to it on its own drop downbeat so the two heavy sections never overlap. Cut lows aggressively to avoid 808 clash.

tracks.why: Defining dubstep with a clear build and a huge drop, perfect for practicing build-to-drop and drop-swap transitions.

tracks.why: Heavy 808 sub and triplet hats demonstrate half-time feel and the importance of cutting lows to avoid 808 clash.

title: Hip-Hop, Open-Format & Party DJing
skill: Run a hip-hop and open-format party set using quick cuts, doubles and crowd-driven selection.
content:
A different mixing philosophy

Hip-hop and open-format party DJing throw out the long blend. These tracks are vocal-led songs people know word for word, not loopy DJ tools — so the goal is to keep the hits coming, play the parts the crowd wants, and get out before they get bored. A wedding or club open-format set might cross from 90s hip-hop to current pop to reggaeton to a house edit in fifteen minutes. The skill is energy, song knowledge, and quick, clean transitions, not 32-bar overlaps.

The core techniques

TechniqueWhat it isWhen
Quick cutCut from one track straight to the next on a downbeatMost transitions — keep momentum
DoublesTwo copies of the same record, cutting between themLoop a hook, scratch, juggle a phrase
Spinback / backspinReverse the platter to slam into the next trackHigh-energy hit changes
Echo-outThrow delay/reverb on the last word and cutSmoothing a tempo or key change
Word/phrase mixingDrop the next track on a lyric the crowd shoutsBig sing-along moments

Mixing songs, not loops

Because these are songs, you mix on the song's structure: the cleanest spots to cut are the start of a verse, a hook, or a breakdown. Many DJs cut on the '1' after a hook, or use the last bar of an a cappella intro to ride into the next track's beat. Tempo varies wildly track to track (a 92 BPM rap song into a 128 house edit), so you are not beatmatching long blends — you are using quick cuts, spinbacks, and echo throws to mask the tempo jump, or relying on edits that have matched intros and outros.

Doubles and the loop

Having two copies of a record — physically on two turntables or two virtual decks — lets you extend a hook indefinitely, juggle a phrase, or scratch over the instrumental. Even without turntablism, looping four bars of an a cappella while you cue the next beat is the open-format equivalent of a blend. A clean 'quick mix' DJ keeps tracks short, often only playing 60-90 seconds of each — the chorus and one verse — then moves.

Read the room, not your plan. Open-format is the most crowd-driven format there is. A pre-built playlist is a starting point you will abandon the moment you see what fills the floor. Watch reactions in real time and follow the energy — the right song at the wrong moment is the wrong song.

Programming and requests

Build mental 'blocks' — a run of 90s hip-hop, a Latin block, a throwback pop block — so you can navigate by vibe and shift the room deliberately. Handle requests by treating them as data about the crowd's taste rather than orders; play the spirit of a request when the literal track would kill the floor. Seize the big sing-along moments: cut the music for a beat and let the crowd carry the hook, then slam the beat back in. That call-and-response is what people remember.

Beat-juggle and scratch flourishes

You do not need to be a battle DJ, but a baby scratch on a transition, a quick cut between doubles, or a juggled hook adds the hands-on energy the format is known for. Keep the gain consistent across wildly different masters so a quiet 90s track does not drop the volume when you cut to it — ride the trim.
exercise: Run a five-song open-format mini-set. Pick five crowd-pleasers across at least three tempos and genres, and transition between them using only quick cuts on the downbeat, one spinback, and one echo-out throw — no long blends. Cut at least one song on a hook so the crowd would carry the vocal, and ride the trim to keep all five at matched volume.

title: Mixing Across Tempos & Genres
skill: Bridge different tempos and scenes using half-time/double-time tricks to mix across genres seamlessly.
content:
Why tempo is not a wall

The single most useful realization in genre-bending DJing is that many genres share a feel at exactly half or double each other's tempo. A 70 BPM hip-hop beat and a 140 BPM dubstep track feel the same — the dubstep is just the hip-hop counted twice as fast. This half-time/double-time relationship lets you mix across scenes that look incompatible on the BPM readout but lock together perfectly once you change how you count them.

The half-time / double-time map

Genre ABPMBridges toBPM
Hip-hop / trap (feel)70-75Dubstep140-150
Dubstep140DnB (pitch up + read as double-time)~170-174
Hip-hop (feel)62-65House / techno124-130
Trap140 grid / 70 feelHip-hop70-90

The core tricks

  1. Half-time / double-time blend: set both software grids correctly, then mix a 140 track over a 70 track — the kicks still align because the slower track's beat falls on every other beat of the fast one. The crowd hears the same pulse at two densities.
  2. Tempo ramp: pull a track's pitch up or down across a long blend to drag the BPM toward the next track's. Modern key-lock keeps it from sounding chipmunked over a range of roughly plus or minus six percent before artefacts show.
  3. Drum bridge: mix only the drum sections of both tracks (intros and outros), where there is no melody to clash, then swap on a phrase — the most reliable cross-genre transition.
  4. FX bridge: echo-out the outgoing track into a beat of silence, then drop the incoming one at a totally different tempo. The gap resets the ear so the tempo jump is not jarring.
  5. Acapella over a new bed: drop a vocal from genre A over an instrumental from genre B at a compatible tempo — a hip-hop a cappella over a house beat is a classic open-format and remix move.
Grid both tracks at their TRUE tempo. Half-time tricks fall apart if your software has analyzed a 140 dubstep track as 70 or a 174 DnB track as 87. Check and fix beatgrids before the gig so the BPM readout reflects the real grid — then you can do the doubling math in your head with confidence.

Worked example: house to DnB

To jump from a 126 house set into DnB, you do not slam to 174. Ramp the house track up to 128-130 across a phrase, then use the drum-only outro to bring in a DnB track whose 174 grid feels like an 87 half-time pulse — close enough to the doubled house feel that the floor follows. Alternatively, echo-out the house track and drop the DnB cold on a fresh 16-bar drum intro; the energy lift sells the jump.

Selling the transition

Cross-genre mixing succeeds on confidence and timing, not on perfect beatmatching. A clean cut on the downbeat of a recognizable new track reads as intentional; a sloppy long blend across a tempo gap reads as a mistake. Use phrasing — land the new genre on a phrase boundary — and use energy direction: jump genres at a moment the floor wants a lift, never during a lull where the change feels random.
exercise: Bridge two genres using the half-time trick. Grid a 70 BPM hip-hop or trap track and a 140 BPM dubstep or house track at their true tempos, then blend the 140 track over the 70 track on the drum sections so the kicks align at double density, and swap on a phrase. Then try the reverse: echo-out one track into a one-beat gap and drop the other cold to feel how the gap masks a tempo jump.
